Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

pair noun

two of a kind taken together

also a pair of, pairs, in pairs, two by two, two each

classical

Cic. Lael. 15: tria aut quattuor … paria amīcōrum
Ov. M. 13.833: pār columbārum (Lewis & Short)
Traupman 113, 356: pār soccōrum, duo paria digitālium

pār, paris n.

noun, third declension, neuter; plural paria

a pair, a couple

The neuter noun of the adjective pār, “equal” (see equal): two that match, of animals, things or people (a pair of friends, of gladiators, of brothers). Things that come in pairs are often simply plural in Latin: calceī are shoes or a pair of shoes; pār is used when the pairs are counted (Traupman 114: duo paria digitālium).

Other words

  • bīnī, bīnae, bīna — two at a time, two each; two (with plural-only nouns)

    distributive numeral, plural · also used · classical · Cic. Att. 7.14.2: distribuit bīnōs singulīs patribus familiārum (Lewis & Short); Cic. Att. 6.1.9: bīnae (litterae), two letters (Lewis & Short)

    In pairs, two to each. With a noun used only in the plural, or with a different sense there, it stands for duo: bīnae litterae are two letters (epistles), duae litterae two letters of the alphabet (Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • ex omnibus saeculīs vix tria aut quattuor nōminantur paria amīcōrum

    from all the ages hardly three or four pairs of friends are namedCic. Lael. 15

  • Quīntī prōgeniēs Arrī, pār nōbile frātrum

    the sons of Quintus Arrius, a famous pair of brothersHor. S. 2.3.243

See also equal, couple, couple, double, shoe, slippers, trousers.

SourcesLewis & Short: par · Lewis & Short: bini

John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 113–114, 356.
